outputs.L1: How can we know that Adam and Eve were happy, deprived as they were of any childhood? Unlike Adam, Eve never knew a world free from the chatter of others. How did she cope? No exit pollster ever thought to ask how she felt as she left at the end of the picture.
outputs.L2: Can we really assume Eve and Adam lived in contentment, considering neither of them ever experienced being a child? Adam, at least, had once existed in a place untroubled by anyone else's talking—but Eve never had that luxury. So how did she manage? And even supposing she'd longed for solitude, what were her options for achieving it? What exactly had Adam consumed that left him hearing voices in his head, all while Eve found herself discovering what frustration meant? Was there anywhere she could escape to for peace from the noise of him—Himself, dressed in nothing but his own hide like some Tarzan figure, announcing to the wilderness that he'd somehow delivered a woman into being? Did she grin at his foolishness, or point out that he'd been fast asleep at the moment she'd arrived and stumbled upon him? Was there any place she might flee to escape his craving for a maternal figure? (What a shame she'd roused him at all.) For the two of them, existence resembled an instructional film unspooling in actual time—a lesson in the meditative art of tending a zoo. So when the door-to-door encyclopedia salesman showed up, who could fault her for making a purchase? And when the film finally ended and she walked out, not a single survey-taker bothered to ask her how she was feeling.
outputs.L3:
# Adam and Eve: A Critical Reimagining

The portrayal of Adam and Eve raises profound questions about the very possibility of their happiness. Unlike ordinary human beings, they are depicted as figures who never experienced a genuine childhood—that formative period of growth, discovery, and gradual self-understanding. Without this foundational stage of life, one must wonder whether they could ever have known true contentment, or whether their existence was fundamentally incomplete from the very beginning.

Eve's situation is particularly striking in its limitations. She had no experience of solitude, no encounter with a world untouched by the voices and expectations of others. From the moment of her creation, she was immersed in a reality already defined and populated. She was denied the essential human experience of coming to know herself in quietness, and more importantly, she had no real opportunity to choose a life of her own. Her path was set before she could ever consider alternatives.

The text also casts a satirical eye on Adam's self-importance, particularly his grandiose claim of having "given birth" to Eve. This assertion is exposed as absurd, for Adam was in fact asleep when Eve came into being. Far from being her creator or the one who brought her forth, he was entirely passive during her arrival. It was Eve who discovered *him*, awakening to find him there. The mockery here deflates Adam's inflated sense of his own role and importance.

Furthermore, Eve is portrayed as weighed down by the burden of Adam's dependence upon her. Rather than being an equal companion, she is cast in the role of a mother figure—someone from whom Adam cannot separate himself and upon whom he relies completely. This dynamic traps Eve in a relationship of caretaking and obligation, one she cannot escape, further diminishing her freedom and autonomy.

Finally, their entire existence is likened to a scripted training film, an artificial scenario in which every outcome seems predetermined. Within this framework, Eve's fateful choice—her decision to buy from the encyclopedia seller, a reimagining of the traditional temptation—is presented not as a sin worthy of blame, but as an entirely understandable act. Given her circumstances, her lack of genuine freedom, and the constraints placed upon her, her choice appears reasonable rather than culpable. The text thus invites us to reconsider the traditional assignment of guilt and to view Eve with sympathy rather than condemnation.
outputs.L4:
# Reimagining Eve

What must it have been to open your eyes already grown, to wake into a body that had never been small? What is it to have no memory of being carried, no recollection of a mother's voice, no scraped knees or first steps or the slow becoming that other creatures know? Eve arrived complete and therefore incomplete—a woman without a girlhood, formed from bone rather than born, cast into existence with no past to steady her and no one who had walked the path before.

Who was there to tell her what she was? Who could she turn to in the long hours when the garden hummed with a peace that felt, to her, more like emptiness? She was alone in a way that Adam could never comprehend, for he at least had been first, had been shaped as the original, had named the animals and claimed a kind of ownership over the world. And what was she to make of him—this man who needed her ceaselessly, who spoke of himself as though the whole of creation revolved around his wanting, who mistook her presence for his possession?

Can we blame her, then, for growing weary? Can we fault her for feeling the walls of paradise close in around her, for sensing that this so-called perfection was in truth a gilded cage? What is Eden to a woman who has no freedom within it, no voice, no history, no companion who truly sees her? The endless days must have stretched before her like a beautiful prison, lovely and suffocating in equal measure.

And so, when the moment came to choose—to reach, to taste, to know—was it truly a fall, or was it an escape? Perhaps she did not sin so much as decide. Perhaps she looked upon the closed circle of that flawless garden and understood that a life without knowledge, without struggle, without the dignity of her own choices, was no life worth keeping. To leave was not weakness but will; not temptation but reason; not the folly of a naive woman seduced, but the deliberate act of one who had had enough.

For too long the story has cast her as the temptress, the weak link, the one through whom ruin entered the world. But what if we have misread her entirely? What if Eve was never the villain but the first to understand that paradise, for her, was a kind of erasure—and that to walk out through its gates was the only way to become fully herself? In granting her this weariness, this loneliness, this hard-won agency, we return to her what the old story stole: her humanity, and with it, our sympathy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a witty, irreverent prose poem reimagining Eve's perspective in the Garden of Eden, questioning whether she and Adam were truly happy without a childhood.
counterfactuals.output:
# On the Question of Whether We Were Ever Children

Consider the peculiar arithmetic of my origin: I arrived pre-assembled, adult and articulate, ribs still warm from their borrowing. No infancy for me. No gummy grin, no first wobbling steps applauded by an audience of angels. I skipped the whole apprenticeship of being small.

And Adam—poor Adam—dust one moment, philosopher the next. Did he ever mispronounce a word? Did he ever fear the dark before he had a name for it? God breathed and *there he was*, fully grown, already bored, naming aardvarks with the weary competence of a man who has never once been surprised.

This is what the sermons omit: we were happy the way furniture is happy. Content, unmarked, without the faintest scratch of memory. No scar to point to and say *here, this is where I learned*. We had no learning. We had only knowing, which is a colder thing, and arrives without the fever of discovery.

I have watched the animals now, and this is my heresy: I envy the fawn its foolishness. I envy the cub its tumble. They earn their grace by first being graceless. But I? I was issued perfection like a uniform, one size fits none, and told to call it Paradise.

So when the serpent came with his glittering proposition, I confess it was not the fruit that tempted me. It was the *before* and *after*. The possibility of an event. The chance to be someone at noon I had not been at dawn.

They call it the Fall. I call it my first childhood—learning, at last, that I could touch a thing and be changed by it. Skinning my innocence like a knee. Weeping my first unscripted tears.

Let the theologians debate my crime. I know only this: I would rather grow up bruised than stay forever new, a woman with no yesterday, smiling in a garden, waiting for something—*anything*—to finally begin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary, satirical monologue that critiques the Adam and Eve creation myth from a feminist angle, using modern imagery like training films and exit pollsters.
counterfactuals.output:
**THE ORIENTATION**

Let me tell you how it really went, because the training film they show you gets it all wrong.

You've seen it, surely. The soft-focus lighting on the apple, the serpent voiced by whoever they hired to make disobedience sound sexy. Cut to Eve, dewy and dumb, reaching. Cut to Adam, wounded fawn, blameless. Cut to the door of the world slamming shut. Roll credits. *Directed by Someone Who Wasn't There.*

I was there. I was, in fact, the entire second act.

Here is the part they edit out. On the first day I could speak, God handed me a laminated card and said, "You are a *helper.*" A helper. Do you know what that word does to a résumé? I have been trying to explain to human resources for six thousand years that "helper" is not a job title, it is a way of describing furniture that occasionally weeps.

And the arrangement—oh, the arrangement was gorgeous on paper. Paradise. All-inclusive. One rule, they said, so simple even a *woman* could follow it. Don't eat from that tree. Fine. Reasonable. Except no one asked me to sign anything. The rule predated me. I arrived to a garden with a mortgage already on it, a covenant I hadn't voted on, drafted by a committee of exactly one, ratified by a rib that couldn't read.

This is my first objection, and I'd like it entered into the minutes.

Now. The serpent. Everyone wants the serpent to be Satan, because it's tidier than admitting the serpent was simply the first honest journalist. He didn't tempt me. He *interviewed* me. He asked a follow-up question—"Did God *really* say?"—which is more than anyone in management ever did. I have met exit pollsters with less rigor. And when I answered, when I finally *thought*, out loud, in a garden designed for obedient silence, that was the crime. Not the fruit. The thinking. The fruit was just the ballot I dropped in the box.

And what a box. What a democracy. One tree, one choice, and the moment I exercised it, they told me the poll was rigged and I was the one who rigged it.

But watch—watch how fast the story turns, because this is the masterstroke, this is the part they should teach in schools of propaganda. I hand Adam the fruit. He eats it. Nobody put it in his mouth. He is a fully grown man made from mud and management's own hands, and he eats it like a raccoon at a picnic, and when God comes walking in the cool of the day asking who dropped the ball, my husband—my *helper's* helper—points one trembling finger and says:

"The woman. The woman *You* gave me."

Note the footnote. *The woman You gave me.* He blames me and he blames God in the same breath, and somehow only I get the labor pains. That is not an apology. That is a man reading his own resignation letter and stapling my name to the bottom.

And they *believed* him. That's what kills me. That's the moment the whole training film pivots. Because from then on the voiceover changes. Suddenly I'm not the first thinker, I'm the first defect. The recall notice. Every catechism, every cathedral, every dress code drafted by men who've never met me, all of it traced back to that afternoon like a bad credit score I can't dispute. Six thousand years of women handed a laminated card that says *helper*, and underneath, in fine print: *see: incident, garden, blame, permanent.*

You want to know the true original sin? It wasn't disobedience. It was the reflex. That ancient, godlike, gorgeous reflex to take a thing that goes wrong and find the nearest woman to name it after.

So here is what I'd put in the sequel, if they ever let me near the edit bay.

I'd keep the tree. I'd keep the fruit, the serpent, the follow-up question. But I'd add one scene. God asks, "Who told you that you were naked?" and instead of the whole cowering chorus, instead of the man's finger and the woman's shame, I'd have Eve straighten up—still holding the apple core, mind you, evidence in hand—and say:

"I told myself. For the first time, I told *myself.* And I'd do the polling again."

Roll credits. *Directed, at last, by someone who was there.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of experimental flash fiction that reinterprets the Genesis story, focusing on Eve's boredom, frustration, and desire for solitude.
counterfactuals.output:
# In the Garden, She Waited for Something to End

Eve counts the leaves. There are too many. There are never enough.

*

Adam names things. This is his gift, God says. This is his purpose. Lion, he says, and the lion becomes a sound. Sparrow. River. Stone. Eve watches his mouth make the world smaller, watches everything shrink into its label and go quiet. She wants to un-name something. She wants to hold a thing that has no word yet, that hums with the not-knowing.

*

The problem with paradise: nothing changes. The fig ripens and does not rot. The light comes and softens and comes again. Adam sleeps beside her, his breath a metronome, and she lies awake cataloging the ways she is alone even here, especially here, in the one place where loneliness was supposed to be impossible.

*

She invents a game. She walks to the far edge of the garden, past where Adam's naming reaches, and she does not answer when he calls. *Eve. Eve.* Her name a hook. She lets it pass through her. For an hour she is no one. It is the closest thing to freedom she has found.

*

God asks: *Are you not happy?*

And she wants to say: happiness is a still pond, and I am a thing that wants to be a river.

She says: *Yes.*

*

The serpent does not tempt her. This is the lie they will tell later. The serpent simply *listens*, and in the listening she hears herself think for the first time. What does the fruit taste like? Not the answer—the *question*. The question is the fruit. The wanting is the fall. She was falling long before her hand moved.

*

Here is what she knows that Adam does not: a garden is also a cage if you cannot leave it. That a gift you did not ask for is a kind of debt. That she would rather have one hour of her own grief than an eternity of borrowed peace.

*

She eats.

Not for knowledge. Not for Adam. Not even for God, who is watching, who is always watching, whose attention is the weather she has lived beneath her whole short life.

She eats because she wanted to do one thing that was *hers*. She eats to make something happen. She eats so that time will finally begin to move, so that there will be a *before* and an *after*, so that she can stand at the border of her own life and say: *here, this, I chose this.*

*

Outside the gate, the world is enormous and unnamed and hers.

She does not look back. She has been looking back her whole life, waiting for someone to tell her what she was.

Now she walks into the wordless dark, and for the first time, she does not count anything at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a clever, sardonic reflection on the Garden of Eden that portrays Adam as a needy, foolish man and Eve as the more perceptive of the two.
counterfactuals.output:
# The First Marriage

Consider Adam: freshly minted, still damp with divine spittle, and already lonely. Not lonely for God—no, the Almighty apparently wasn't sufficient company—but lonely in that specific, whining way that would echo through every man who ever sighed heavily until someone asked what was wrong.

So God, that great enabler, performed history's first act of codependency and pulled a woman from Adam's own body, because heaven forbid the man learn to sit with himself for an afternoon.

Enter Eve, who arrived to find a fully-grown adult who had somehow not yet noticed he was naked. Let us pause here. Adam had walked the Garden for who knows how long, naming every creature—*that one's a giraffe, that one's a wombat*—and in all that cataloging, never once glanced downward with curiosity. Eve, by contrast, took one look at the Tree of Knowledge and thought: *Now there's a career opportunity.*

The serpent, we're told, tempted her. But watch how quickly the story reveals its bias. Eve *considered*. She weighed the fruit's merits—"good for food, pleasing to the eye, desirable for gaining wisdom." That's three separate evaluative criteria. That's due diligence. That's a woman making an informed decision.

And Adam? Adam ate it because she handed it to him. No deliberation. No serpent required. Just a man accepting food from his wife with the reflexive obedience of a golden retriever. The first human male's contribution to the pivotal moment of theological history was: *okay, sure.*

Then, caught, he offered his masterstroke of accountability: "The woman *you* gave me—she made me do it." One sentence, two people blamed, zero ownership. He threw his wife and his God under the same chariot, and men have been calling *her* the troublemaker ever since.

Eve, at least, ate her apple with her eyes open. Adam is still asking where his rib went.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an original poem or prose passage that questions the assumptions behind the Eden myth, blending biblical references with contemporary pop culture allusions like Tarzan and encyclopedia salesmen.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Salesman at the Gate**

Consider the encyclopedia man,
his sample case of *A through Knowledge*,
knocking at Eden's east gate
where the flaming sword still turns—
volumes bound in serpent-skin,
each entry a fruit, each fruit
a footnote to the fall.

*Would you like to know things?*
he asks, and this, we're told,
was the original sin:
to want the index, the cross-reference,
the marginalia of the world.

But I have questions.

Why plant the tree at all
if not to grow the reaching?
Why give a mouth its hunger
then curse it for the swallow?
The Author placed the apple
like a loaded gun in Act One—
we know the rules of narrative,
we've seen this on the screen.

And Tarzan—consider him,
raised innocent among the vines,
naked and unashamed,
Adam with a jungle yell.
When Jane arrived with buttons
and the Latin names for things,
did he mourn his lost non-knowing?
Did the vine-swing feel like exile?

No. He learned the word for *tree*
and loved the tree the more.
He learned the word for *Jane*
and this was not a curse
but the whole point of the garden—
that a thing might name the thing beside it,
might say *I see you, other,*
might reach across the difference.

So here is my heresy,
sold door to door like brushes,
like the good news of vacuum cleaners:

Perhaps the fruit was always meant.
Perhaps the fall was flight.
Perhaps the God who made the ache
also made the answer—
not the fig leaf, not the shame,
but the encyclopedia's promise
that everything can be looked up,
that ignorance is not a virtue,
only a room we haven't entered yet.

The snake was just a salesman
with a decent product line.
The apple was an appetizer.
And Eden, that closed garden,
was the only prison ever built
whose inmates broke *out*
into the larger world,

blinking, ashamed, alive,
and finally awake enough
to grieve, to build, to name,
to knock on stranger's doors
and offer them the terrible,
the necessary volumes:

*Here is the world. It's heavy.
It costs you everything you had.
You're going to want to read it.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
